title: A household finance agent with limits and read-back
summary: A personal agent that reads email, calendar and bank data, writes calendar events and sheet cells, and reads back every change. Bank data stays read-only, and the agent never moves money.

stat.label: every bill and payoff becomes a calendar event the agent builds and reads back

sections.heading: Problem
paragraphs: A household's money lives in many places: inboxes, calendars, bank apps and lender portals. Due dates slip and promotional deadlines pass unnoticed.

sections.heading: What I built
paragraphs: A personal agent that reads email, calendar, spreadsheets and bank data. Bank data is strictly read-only. The agent writes calendar events and spreadsheet cells, marks mail read, and sends mail to the household's other agent. It cannot move money or change account settings.

It verifies each fact at its source of record before it states a number: the calendar for dates, bank data for balances, the lender's statement for terms. A clearly labelled estimate is the one exception, and it is never presented as verified. After every calendar or sheet change, it fetches the event or row again and reads it back before it calls the work done.

The agent asks me before it sends to anyone outside the household, deletes anything or takes any step that is hard to undo. Two things run on standing authorization instead: mail between the household's two agents, and routine bill logging inside the scheduled sweeps. Mail between the agents uses a header block that names sender, topic, type and date. Logins stay in a secure vault and never appear in chat or mail.
Every bill and payoff is a dated calendar event.

sections.heading: Result
paragraphs: The agent keeps every dated bill and payoff row in one tracker sheet.
It sweeps the inbox several times a day. Volume varies from a couple of messages to a busy pile. In its first month it built dozens of dated money events, and it has corrected others since.

A handful of payoff checks fire over two months. Each one runs the morning after a due date to confirm the payment posted, then marks it done. The checks verify, and I decide what to pay. I have no time measurement behind an hours-saved figure, so I do not claim one.

sections.heading: What went wrong
paragraphs: The agent once gave me the wrong due date for a payment. It took the date from a stale tracker row, while the calendar showed a later date. It corrected the date the same day. The rule since is calendar first, tracker second: it never states a date or amount from the tracker alone.
Silent sweep runs taught a second rule: no report means failure, so a sweep that finishes owes a summary without being asked.

sections.heading: Lesson
paragraphs: Limit what the agent can do, and name the exceptions, before you tune how well it does it. Verify at the source of record and read every change back, so mistakes are cheap to catch. An agent that can write, send and mark mail read is still safe to run when each of those has a check and a stated limit.

sources: the agent's own audit reply, 2026-11-03 (permissions, sweep schedule, ordering, counts, checks, the wrong-date incident)
